name: Uttarey
tagline: A Limbu border village under the Singalila Ridge
meta_description: Uttarey guide: Singshore Bridge, the Singalila Ridge and Chiwa Bhanjyang trail, trout farm, Limbu villages, homestays, jeeps, costs and permits.
summary: Uttarey is a border village at about 2,000 m in Gyalshing district, under the Singalila Ridge that divides Sikkim from Nepal. It is about 45 km from Pelling via Dentam and Singshore Bridge. Come for forest walks, the ridge trail towards Chiwa Bhanjyang, a trout farm and Limbu village life. One or two nights suits most people.
intro: Uttarey sits at about 2,000 m on the northern slopes of the Singalila Ridge, the long spine of hills that forms the border between Sikkim and Nepal. It is the last sizeable village on this road, at the far western edge of Gyalshing district. Beyond it are temperate forests, rhododendron slopes and the old walking trails up to the ridge. Most visitors are Indian families on a quiet weekend, trekkers, and a few people who simply want to be off the map.

Getting here is half the fun. From Pelling the road drops to Dentam and crosses Singshore Bridge, about 240 m long and roughly 100 m above the gorge, described as the highest bridge in Sikkim. It then climbs again to Uttarey, about 45 km and 2–2.5 hours in all. In the village you will find homestays, small shops, a trout farm, a few monasteries and views towards the Kangchenjunga range on clear days.

Uttarey is home to Limbu (Limboo) and Bhutia families, along with other Nepali-speaking communities. Daily life runs on farming, livestock and, more and more, homestays. For a budget trip it works well: shared jeeps from Gyalshing, simple full-board rooms and free walks. Plan for October to December for clear views, or March to May for flowers on the ridge. The border is close, so carry photo ID at all times.

story.title: A Limbu borderland under the ridge
paras: The Limbu call themselves Yakthung and their language Yakthungpan. Their homeland, Limbuwan, spreads across eastern Nepal and into West Sikkim, and the Singalila Ridge above Uttarey has never been much of a barrier to families on either side. Limbu life follows the Mundhum, an oral body of scripture that guides rituals, marriage and the farming year. Their main festival is Chasok Tangnam, a harvest thanksgiving. Limbu is also one of the official languages of Sikkim.

The Limbu script is linked to the name Sirijunga. Wikipedia credits its first design to a Limbu king of that name, and in the 18th century the scholar Te-ongsi Sirijunga Xin Thebe worked to revive the script and teach it. He was killed at Martam in West Sikkim. Today the script is taught again in schools in Sikkim, and you may spot it on signboards and in prayer books in Limbu homes around Uttarey.

Above the village, trails climb to the Singalila Ridge and the border pass of Chiwa Bhanjyang, bhanjyang being the Nepali word for a pass. For generations people walked these routes between Sikkim and Nepal for trade, marriage and grazing. Today the pass has an SSB post, and walkers need ID and a local guide. We cannot confirm the current rules for crossing there, so treat it as a ridge walk, not a border crossing, and check current status before you travel.

did_you_know: Singshore Bridge, on the road from Pelling to Uttarey, is about 240 m long and about 100 m high, and links the Dentam and Uttarey sides of a gorge.
The Limbu people call themselves Yakthung and follow the Mundhum, an oral scripture that guides their rituals.
The 18th-century Limbu scholar Te-ongsi Sirijunga Xin Thebe, who worked to spread the Limbu script, was killed at Martam in West Sikkim.
facts: Singshore Bridge, Singalila trails, trout farm

highlights.title: Singshore Bridge
highlights.text: About 240 m long and roughly 100 m above the gorge, Singshore links the Dentam and Uttarey sides of the valley and is called the highest bridge in Sikkim. Walk across it on foot; it is free or nominal, and the drop is something to see.

highlights.title: The Singalila Ridge
highlights.text: Uttarey lies on the northern slopes of the ridge that divides Sikkim from Nepal. Trails climb through oak, magnolia and rhododendron forest towards the border pass of Chiwa Bhanjyang. Go with a local guide, carry ID and start at dawn.

highlights.title: Trout farm
highlights.text: Uttarey has a trout farm, a small, practical place where fish are reared in clear cold water. It is a short, easy stop for families, and some homestays can cook fresh trout for dinner if you ask a day ahead.

highlights.title: Limbu and Bhutia village life
highlights.text: Uttarey is home to Limbu and Bhutia families. Walk the lanes, look for prayer flags and Limbu script on signboards, and accept a cup of tea if offered. Homestays here are the easiest way to meet people and eat home food.

highlights.title: Rhododendrons in spring
highlights.text: From March to May the forests above the village turn red and pink with rhododendron flowers, the same bloom that draws walkers to nearby Barsey. Higher up the ridge, flowering can run into May. Bring a rain jacket for afternoon showers.

highlights.title: Quiet, cheap and off the circuit
highlights.text: Few tour groups come this far, so rooms are simple and prices modest. Homestays with all meals cost roughly ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, indicative, 2026. Walks, the bridge and the views are free. Come in November or March for the quietest weeks.

how_to_reach.text: From Siliguri or Gangtok, take a shared jeep to Gyalshing (₹400–550 or ₹350–500 a seat). From Gyalshing, a few jeeps a day run to Dentam and Uttarey; expect roughly ₹100–200 a seat, indicative, 2026. Most leave in the morning or around midday, so reach Gyalshing early and check current status before you travel.

From Pelling a reserved car costs about ₹2,500–3,500 one way for the 45 km, 2–2.5 hour run via Singshore Bridge, indicative, 2026. From NJP or Bagdogra it is a long 7–8 hour day; most people break the journey at Pelling. Ask the driver to stop at the bridge.

Bagdogra (IXB) and New Jalpaiguri (NJP), both in Siliguri, are the nearest airport and main railhead. Pelling is about 140–150 km and 5–6.5 hours from either, and Uttarey a further 2–2.5 hours. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Uttarey has a handful of family homestays and small lodges spread around the village and along the road. Rooms are simple, often with wooden floors, thick quilts and hot water by geyser or bucket. Most hosts serve all meals: rice, dal, local greens, eggs or chicken, and trout if you ask in advance. Expect about ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day with meals, indicative, 2026. There are no big hotels here. If you want more comfort, sleep in Pelling and come for a long day trip, but you lose the early start for ridge walks.
costs: Local guide for a ridge walk
budget_tip: Ride the shared jeep from Gyalshing instead of hiring a car from Pelling, and you save ₹2,000 or more each way for the price of an early start.
tips: Carry photo ID everywhere, as SSB and police posts near the Nepal border may check it.
Start ridge walks at dawn; cloud usually rolls up the valleys by late morning.
Tell your homestay a day ahead if you want trout for dinner.
Withdraw cash in Gyalshing or Pelling, because ATMs and card machines are scarce in Uttarey.
Avoid June to September, when rain, leeches and landslides make the Dentam road slow; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Walk across Singshore Bridge
experiences.summary: Stop on the Pelling–Uttarey road and walk across Singshore Bridge, about 240 m long and roughly 100 m above the gorge. It is called the highest bridge in Sikkim, costs little or nothing and takes under an hour.
body: Singshore Bridge spans a deep gorge between the Dentam and Uttarey sides of the valley. Wikipedia gives it a length of about 240 m and a height of about 100 m, and calls it the highest bridge in Sikkim. It was built in the early 2000s to save villagers a long detour down to the river and back up. Today it is also a favourite stop for travellers heading to Uttarey from Pelling.

Ask your driver to park at one end, then walk across and back. On a clear day you look down to the river far below and out over forested slopes with waterfalls after rain. The bridge carries vehicles, so stay to the side and watch for jeeps. It can sway a little in the wind, which children love and some adults do not. Hold small children's hands, and do not lean over the railings for selfies.

Morning light is best for photos, and the bridge is quietest before about 10 am. There is usually no fee, though a small charge or parking fee may be collected in season, so keep change handy. Snack stalls may be open at busy times, but do not count on it. If heights bother you, the view from the end is almost as good as from the middle. Allow 30–45 minutes in all, including photos.

faqs.q: How high is Singshore Bridge
faqs.a: Singshore Bridge is about 100 m above the gorge and about 240 m long, according to Wikipedia, which calls it the highest bridge in Sikkim. Some local signs and websites make bigger claims about its ranking in Asia, but the figures above are the ones we use.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Singshore Bridge
faqs.a: Usually not. Crossing on foot is free, though a small parking or entry charge may be collected at busy times. Keep ₹20–50 in change just in case, indicative, 2026. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel and follow any local instructions.

faqs.q: How far is Singshore Bridge from Pelling
faqs.a: The bridge lies on the road from Pelling to Uttarey via Dentam. Pelling to Uttarey is about 45 km and 2–2.5 hours, and the bridge comes in the later part of the drive. Most people combine it with a night in Uttarey rather than a rushed day trip.

experiences.title: Singalila Ridge trail towards Chiwa Bhanjyang
experiences.duration: Full day, or 2–4 days as a trek
experiences.best_time: Oct–Dec for views, Apr–May for rhododendrons
experiences.summary: Climb from Uttarey through temperate forest towards the Singalila Ridge and the border pass of Chiwa Bhanjyang. It is a long, steep day with a local guide, or the start of a multi-day ridge trek. Carry ID and start at first light.
body: The Singalila Ridge runs north–south along the border between Nepal and India, from the Darjeeling hills into West Sikkim. Uttarey sits on its northern slopes, and old trails climb from the village to the border pass at Chiwa Bhanjyang. Bhanjyang is the Nepali word for a pass. Local people used these routes for generations to move between Sikkim and Nepal for trade, family visits and grazing. Many of those paths are still in daily use.

The walk climbs steadily through oak, magnolia and rhododendron forest, with clearings that open views back over West Sikkim. Distances and timings depend on how far you go and how fit you are, so we do not quote a fixed figure. Plan a full day for a return walk with a local guide. Longer treks continue along the ridge in Sikkim towards Phoktey Dara and Barsey and need tents or huts and a registered operator.

The pass has an SSB border post. Indian walkers should carry photo ID; foreign nationals should not attempt this route without an operator who has confirmed what is allowed. We cannot confirm current crossing rules, so do not plan to enter Nepal here, and check current status before you travel. Weather turns fast on the ridge: carry a warm layer, rain shell, water and food. Leave early, turn back by early afternoon, and tell your homestay your plan.

faqs.q: Can I cross into Nepal at Chiwa Bhanjyang
faqs.a: Do not plan on it. Chiwa Bhanjyang is a border pass with an SSB post, and we cannot confirm that it is open as a crossing for tourists. Foreign nationals in particular should cross only at authorised border points. Treat the pass as a ridge walk and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Singalila trail from Uttarey
faqs.a: Yes, we strongly suggest one. Trails split in the forest, signs are few, cloud comes in fast and the border is close. A local guide costs about ₹1,000–1,800 a day, indicative, 2026, and can also explain the plants, birds and village stories along the way.

faqs.q: When is the best time for the Uttarey ridge walk
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest views of the snow peaks and dry trails. April and May bring rhododendron flowers on the ridge but more haze and afternoon showers. January and February can bring snow higher up. Avoid June to September, when the forest is wet and full of leeches.

experiences.title: Trout farm and Uttarey village walk
experiences.summary: An easy afternoon around Uttarey: the trout farm, small monasteries, prayer flags and farm lanes, finished with tea at your homestay. Order fresh trout for dinner a day ahead. It suits families and anyone who needs a gentle day after the drive.
body: Uttarey has a trout farm, where fish are reared in tanks fed by clear, cold mountain water. It is not a theme park, just a working place, but children enjoy seeing the fish, and it shows how villages here make use of their streams. Ask your homestay how to get there and whether a visit is fine on the day. Keep to the paths around the tanks. A small fee may apply; ask first.

From the farm, wander back through the village. Look for small monasteries and chortens, prayer flags on bamboo poles, and Limbu script on signboards and doors. Fields of maize, potato and vegetables fill the slopes in season, and cattle graze at the forest edge. Greet people with a namaste and ask before you take photos of anyone, especially older villagers and children. Late afternoon light is soft and good for photos.

Back at your homestay, ask if trout can be cooked for dinner. Most hosts need a day's notice, and the price is extra, so agree it in advance. A simple fried or curried trout with rice and greens is the taste of Uttarey. The walk itself is free, flat to gently hilly, and fine for seniors who take it slowly with rests. Bring a light jacket, because the air cools fast after 4 pm.

faqs.q: Is there a trout farm in Uttarey
faqs.a: Yes. Uttarey has a trout farm where fish are reared in cold mountain water. It is a working farm rather than a big attraction, so visits are short and informal. Ask your homestay about access and timings, and whether fresh trout can be cooked for your dinner.

faqs.q: Can I eat trout in Uttarey
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many homestays can cook trout if you ask a day ahead, as they need to source it fresh. Expect it to cost extra over the standard full-board rate. Prices vary by host and season, so agree the amount before they cook.

faqs.q: What else is there to do in Uttarey for families
faqs.a: Families can walk across Singshore Bridge, visit the trout farm, stroll to small monasteries and spend time on homestay terraces with views on clear days. Older children can manage a short forest walk with a guide. There are no malls or rides, so it suits families who like quiet.

experiences.title: Homestay evening with a Limbu family
experiences.summary: Spend an evening by the kitchen fire with a Limbu or Bhutia host family in Uttarey. Eat home-cooked food, ask about the Mundhum, Limbu script and life on the border, and go to bed early for a dawn start.
body: Uttarey is home to Limbu and Bhutia families, and staying with one is the best way to understand the village. The Limbu call themselves Yakthung. Their traditions follow the Mundhum, an oral scripture recited by priests at births, weddings and funerals, and their main festival is Chasok Tangnam, a thanksgiving for the harvest. Limbu is one of the official languages of Sikkim. Your hosts may be Limbu, Bhutia or Nepali-speaking; every home is different.

Dinner is usually simple and filling: rice, dal, seasonal greens, a pickle, perhaps chicken or pork. Ask about kinema, the fermented soybean dish that Limbu kitchens are known for, and about tongba, millet beer sipped through a bamboo straw, if your hosts make it. Do not push if they do not. Eat with your right hand if you like, and praise the cook. Say so early if you are vegetarian or avoid alcohol; hosts are used to it and will cook accordingly.

Ask questions with care: how the family came to Uttarey, what crops they grow, what festivals they keep. Some homes have prayer books or calendars in Limbu script; ask before you photograph them. Evenings end early here, often by 9 pm, because farm days start at dawn. That suits you too if you plan a ridge walk in the morning. Pay your bill the night before if you leave at dawn, and carry small notes.

faqs.q: Who are the Limbu people of Sikkim
faqs.a: The Limbu, who call themselves Yakthung, are an indigenous people of eastern Nepal and Sikkim. Their homeland is known as Limbuwan. They follow the Mundhum, an oral scripture, have their own script linked to the name Sirijunga, and celebrate Chasok Tangnam. In Sikkim they are recognised as a Scheduled Tribe.

faqs.q: What food will I eat at an Uttarey homestay
faqs.a: Expect rice, dal, seasonal greens, pickles, eggs and chicken or pork, served at breakfast and dinner, often with lunch too. Ask about kinema, a fermented soybean dish, and fresh trout a day ahead. Vegetarian meals are easy to arrange if you say so when booking.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay at a homestay in Uttarey
faqs.a: Yes, homestays in Uttarey are family homes and generally safe for solo travellers, women and families. Book through a known contact or your operator, share your plans with someone, and carry ID. Rooms are basic, so bring a torch, warm socks and any medicines you need.

faqs.q: Is Uttarey worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for travellers who want a quiet border village with forest walks rather than sights. Uttarey offers Singshore Bridge on the way, ridge trails towards Chiwa Bhanjyang, a trout farm, Limbu village life and cheap homestays. One or two nights is right. If you need restaurants and shops, base yourself in Pelling instead.

faqs.q: How far is Uttarey from Pelling
faqs.a: Uttarey is about 45 km from Pelling, a drive of 2–2.5 hours via Dentam and Singshore Bridge. A reserved car costs roughly ₹2,500–3,500 one way, indicative, 2026. By shared jeep, go to Gyalshing first and take one of the few daily jeeps towards Dentam and Uttarey.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Uttarey
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit for Uttarey, but carry photo ID, because SSB and police posts near the Nepal border may check it. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit and should ask an operator about any extra rules near the border. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Uttarey
faqs.a: October to December brings clear skies, dry trails and the best views. March to May brings rhododendrons on the slopes above the village, with more haze and some showers. January and February are cold and may bring snow higher up. June to September is monsoon, with slow roads and leeches.

faqs.q: How cold is Uttarey in winter
faqs.a: At about 2,000 m, Uttarey is cold from December to February, with frosty nights and chilly mornings; snow is possible on the ridge above. Homestays give thick quilts, but heating is rare. Pack thermals, a down or fleece jacket, a cap and warm socks, and expect hot water by bucket.

faqs.q: Can I trek from Uttarey to Sandakphu
faqs.a: The Singalila Ridge links Uttarey with the trails towards Phalut and Sandakphu in the Darjeeling hills, but this means crossing between states along a border with Nepal. Routes, permits and rules change, so do it only with a registered operator who arranges permits, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Uttarey
faqs.a: There is usually mobile coverage in the village, though it can be weak in bad weather and drops on the ridge trails. Near the border your phone may pick up a Nepali network, so switch off data roaming to avoid charges. Download offline maps before you leave Pelling.

faqs.q: How do I combine Uttarey with other places
faqs.a: A good loop is Pelling, Uttarey via Singshore Bridge, then south to Rinchenpong, Okhrey or Barsey before heading to Darjeeling via Jorethang. Give it four or five nights. Ask your driver about road conditions on the link roads, which are narrow and can close after heavy rain.

faqs.q: Is Uttarey good for a budget trip
faqs.a: Yes. Shared jeeps from Gyalshing cost about ₹100–200 a seat, homestays with all meals run roughly ₹1,200–2,000 per person per day, and the bridge, village and forest walks are free, all indicative, 2026. The main extra cost is a guide for ridge walks, which is worth paying for.
